items.title: Why Christians Must Prepare For ‘Information Warfare’
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: Important.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

A communications expert who specializes in Generation Z and Christian communications is warning there’s an informational battle unfolding that believers must pay attention to — and that fears of new technologies must be tempered.

Listen to the latest episode of “Quick Start”

“New media is something we shouldn’t be afraid of,” Bethany Miller, communications director for National Religious Broadcasters, told CBN News, explaining that people both young and old are relying on social media for information and news gathering. “We need to stay ahead of the curve and realize new media is the way. Social media is how we get our headlines.”

Miller knows the pitfalls that can come from getting news from Reels and short videos, discussing how younger people are even more tuned in to social media for these purposes.

“Today’s Gen Z’s … and … teenagers … are growing up without any form of separation between the digital and the physical,” she said. “And so information is being consumed … and then the tricky part is now we’re having the question of: ‘What is real and what is not real?'”

This complicates how people process information around war and major news events, and with artificial intelligence emerging it only adds to the chaos and confusion. As a result, there’s an “information warfare” of sorts taking form.

“We’re having a type of access that’s misinformation and we’re getting headlines that are not accurate,” she said. “We’re getting everyone’s opinion and … we don’t need everyone’s opinion because now we’re having both truth and untruth and now Gen Z has a barrage — the American public as a whole has a barrage — of headlines.”

Miller continued, “And now you have to do the discernment of what is true, what is not true, and my concern is that Gen Z has not grown up with that distance between what is reality and what is not reality.”

The assumption that random videos and AI-generated content are true is creating a plethora of confusion, she said.

“Gen Z doesn’t have that type of discernment that they need to realize whether or not something is true, whether something is biblical, whether something is true, good and beautiful,” Miller said.

Despite this dynamic, she described being encouraged by how Christians are stepping into social media, film, TV, and other forms of entertainment, offering quality content. For a long time, Christian entertainment was criticized for a lack of excellence, but Miller believes those tides are changing.

“Christian media is paving the way, but we still have quite a lot more work to do,” she said, noting it’s important for Christians to get a better grip on the audience. “I think we’re starting to see that, but we still have a long way to go. We need to make sure that we know our audience. We know that 30 seconds is what performs well on Instagram. We need to know that we need to format.”

Miller added, “We know that Christian media has the answer, we have truth, we are the only ones that are providing the way to eternity.”

Part of engaging, she said, is understanding that we’re in a spiritual war that requires engagement. She cited examples of persecution in Nigeria not getting much coverage — and of Israel being maligned after Hamas’ deadly October 7 terror attacks.

“The mission field is different today,” Miller said. “When we talk about the Great Commission, that doesn’t just mean going over across seas to Africa; it also means getting online because the mission field is also media. It is also digital.”

And that digital world, much like the physical, demands that Christians take action.

“The digital world is a spiritual world as well and Christians need to be there combating, and we need to be there leading the front lines, and we need to be there getting the truth,” she said.

items.title: PRAY: Hikers Disappear as Severe Flooding Slams the Grand Canyon
items.author: Tré Goins-Phillips
items.summary: "Public assistance requested"
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

At least one person is dead and more than a dozen missing after flash flooding overwhelmed a remote area of the Grand Canyon on Saturday, according to National Park Service officials.

“The National Park Service is asking the public to provide information for more than 20 individuals who may be missing or unaccounted for following a significant flash flood in Bright Angel Canyon and the Phantom Ranch area on August 29,” reads a Facebook post from the Grand Canyon National Park.

At least one 46-year-old man was killed during the flooding and his body was found around Crystal Rapids. Authorities warned more severe weather could hit the area Monday. As of Sunday night, around 15 people were still missing or unaccounted for.

The devastating flooding over the weekend hammered Bright Angel Canyon and Phantom Ranch, both of which are located deep within the Grand Canyon, on Saturday. Bright Angel Canyon, a major side canyon, runs roughly 10 miles from the North Rim down to the Colorado River, and Phantom Ranch sits at the bottom of the inner canyon, slightly north of the Colorado River.

Both areas were closed Saturday after the torrential rainfall, with more than 62 people evacuated Sunday morning.

“The flash flood resulted in significant impacts to infrastructure throughout Bright Angel Canyon,” the NPS explained. “Nearly all footbridges spanning Bright Angel Creek were destroyed, eliminating hiker access across the creek.”

Park officials also said the Colorado River would be closed to river traffic “until further notice” because of metal structures and debris entering the waterway. Those already in the canyon, the NPS said, “are receiving direction through river operations rangers and the Grand Canyon River Alert system.”

David Gregory, one of the hikers who was evacuated, told Arizona’s Family he would not have survived without the help of his rescuers. The water was moving so quickly, Gregory said, that, without help, it would have been “game over” for him.

“I definitely think we could have gotten caught up in that side creek, and if we would have fallen in or the water carried us in, I think it would have been game over,” he told the local news outlet. “Because that creek was moving so quickly, there was so many rocks and tree branches and then, once you get into the Colorado River, it was like a whirlpool in there with all the debris circling around.”

On Sunday, the NPS announced stage 4 water restrictions beginning Monday, revealing the severe weather caused “extensive damage to inner canyon infrastructure, including the Transcanyon Waterline, which supplies water from the canyon to the park.”

For the “foreseeable future,” only dry camping is permitted, fires are restricted, and visitors and residents have been asked to shower for five minutes maximum and to “flush toilets selectively.”

Pray for those still missing, for the rangers and volunteers working to rescue them, and for their loved ones.

items.title: Christ in Me
items.author: Jennifer Benson Schuldt
items.summary: Renaissance artist Albrecht Dürer became famous for his talent at age twenty. The art critics of his day called him “the greatest mind that ever expressed itself in line.” As his fame spread, influential people tried to hire him with promises of luxury and ease. Even other acclaimed
items.content:
📖 Devotional | Our Daily Bread

Renaissance artist Albrecht Dürer became famous for his talent at age twenty. The art critics of his day called him “the greatest mind that ever expressed itself in line.” As his fame spread, influential people tried to hire him with promises of luxury and ease. Even other acclaimed artists such as Giovanni Bellini and Raphael revered his work.

In what experts consider to be his best self-portrait, Dürer mingled his physical characteristics with what he thought Jesus might have looked like. He painted himself with long wavy hair, a beard, and eyes that seemed to convey a sense of divine purpose. Many assumed this piece was a prideful statement about the artist’s opinion of himself. Others who were familiar with his virtuous character believed the painting wasn’t blasphemous or big-headed but aspirational. They believed Dürer wanted to live a life that would allow people to see Jesus in him.

If we truly know Christ, this is our desire as well. Believing in Him and accepting His death and resurrection as the basis for our relationship with God means we should now live for Jesus—not for ourselves (Galatians 2:19). We live for Him and He lives in us and works through us. The apostle Paul said this about his spiritual transformation: “I no longer live, but Christ lives in me” (v. 20). May the glory of Christ shine through our lives today so that the world sees Him in us.

items.title: ‘Time’ Says There Isn’t a Gen Z Revival. The Data Backs Them Up — But They Looked in the Wrong Rooms.
items.author: RELEVANT
items.summary: Time magazine ran a piece this month asking whether there’s a religious revival happening among Gen Z. It opens on a 23-year-old named Anthony Gross who moved to New York, didn’t know anyone, started ranking Catholic churches on TikTok, and walked into a packed Sunday mass in Greenwich V
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

Time magazine ran a piece this month asking whether there’s a religious revival happening among Gen Z. It opens on a 23-year-old named Anthony Gross who moved to New York, didn’t know anyone, started ranking Catholic churches on TikTok, and walked into a packed Sunday mass in Greenwich Village where he says everybody was under 30.

Then it asks the researchers, and they say no.

About 25% of Americans report attending church weekly. Move that to 28% — three points — and you have added 12 million people.

Ryan Burge, a political scientist who has become the designated skeptic in every one of these stories, ran that out for us. There are roughly 300,000 Christian churches in America, so 12 million people means every one of them adds 35 to 40 faces that weren’t there a year ago. The average American church runs about 70 on a Sunday. That church goes to 110, and stays.

“How many stories have you heard of a church that’s 75 people now is 125 people?” Burge told RELEVANT. “I’ve not heard any.”

That’s the modest version. Nobody is describing it because it isn’t happening. So Time got the big thing right. What they got wrong is narrower: almost every scene in the article is Catholic.

The TikToker ranks Catholic parishes. The bishop is the Diocese of Phoenix. Three of the four gatherings they cite are Catholic youth conferences. That’s a strange way to describe a generation that is overwhelmingly not Catholic.

The one evangelical data point they include, they drop. Passion, the largest conference for 18-to-25-year-olds, is expanding into two stadiums for the first time in its history — Texas in December, Georgia in February. That’s 120,000 Gen Z attendees, and it gets a clause.

Bishop Dolan’s hundreds of Easter baptisms, most of them Gen Z, get the same treatment. If the argument is that the anecdotes don’t add up to a trend, the anecdotes are worth gathering first.

There’s also a number doing work it can’t do. Time cites PRRI finding more than 75% of Americans over 65 identify as Christian against 54% of adults under 30, and offers it as evidence against a resurgence. That gap isn’t new and it isn’t a direction. Young people have been less religious than old people for as long as anyone has measured it, and the distance between two age groups says nothing about which way either is moving. The decline stopped.

For 30 years every survey of American religion pointed the same way, down, generation over generation. That’s no longer true.

The share of Gen Z claiming no religious affiliation has flattened around 42%. The religiosity gap between millennials and Gen Z is roughly half the gap between millennials and Gen X, or Gen X and boomers. Pew finds people born in the 1990s and people born in the early 2000s look about the same.

Burge won’t give an inch on the word revival and gives that much. He puts the country’s floor at about 45% Christian, 45% unaffiliated, 10% everything else. “That’s still an amazingly Christian country for a Western democracy to be,” he said.

A generation that was supposed to keep falling stopped falling. Nobody posts about it, because it doesn’t come with a stadium photo. It’s also the first floor anyone has found in three decades.

Both things are true at once, and holding both is harder than picking one. There’s no national revival. There are also full rooms, and they aren’t imaginary — Burge allows the pockets of growth even while the macro number sits flat.

The move to avoid is the one that’s been everywhere this year: finding the single survey that points the right direction and treating it as settled.

“I got one poll over here is not extraordinary evidence, folks,” Burge said. “It’s cherry picking.”

The people filling those rooms don’t need the national number to move. It would be nice, eventually, if it did.

items.title: Blessed Is He: The Life and Legacy of Archbishop Fulton J. Sheen
items.author: Dr. Richard DeClue
items.summary:
Dr. Richard DeClue

Ven. Fulton J. Sheen will be beatified on September 24, 2026. Here is an overview of this holy bishop’s life and accomplishments.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Dr. Richard DeClue

Ven. Fulton J. Sheen will be beatified on September 24, 2026, in St. Louis, Missouri. As a fan of Archbishop Fulton Sheen since my childhood, I was thrilled to hear this news! Looking forward to that event, I would like to give an overview of this holy bishop’s life and accomplishments. 

Fulton Sheen was born in El Paso, IL, in 1895. I only recently learned from the Archbishop Fulton J. Sheen Foundation that his given name at birth was actually Peter John Sheen. However, while still a child, he began to be called Fulton, which was his mother’s maiden name. He was raised in the Catholic faith and was always devoted to Our Blessed Mother.

Fulton was high school valedictorian, graduating from Spalding Institute (a Catholic high school in Peoria, IL) in 1913. Thereafter, he attended St. Viator College before becoming a seminarian for the Diocese of Peoria. He was ordained to the priesthood on September 20, 1919. The next year, he began further studies at the Catholic University of America (CUA), earning an ecclesiastical degree in canon law (J.C.B.). The following year, he moved to the Catholic University of Louvain (Belgium), where he earned a PhD in philosophy in 1923, winning the Cardinal Mercier Prize for International Philosophy. In 1924, he earned the degree of Doctor of Sacred Theology at the Pontifical University of St. Thomas Aquinas in Rome (a.k.a., the Angelicum).

According to the Encyclopedia Britannica, Sheen then spent another year of study in Belgium, followed by a year of priestly ministry in London. He returned to his home diocese and worked as a parish priest in 1926. That same year, however, he joined the faculty at CUA.

As the university’s Fulton Sheen biography states: “For the next 23 years, Catholic University was where Father Sheen honed his skills as a scholar, educator, orator and evangelist. He worked, first in the School of Theology and Religious Studies, then in the School of Philosophy.” He taught courses such as “Philosophy of Religion,” “God and Society,” and “God and Modern Philosophy.” During this time, he was given the title of monsignor by Pope Pius XI in 1934 at the age of thirty-nine.

While still undertaking his professorial duties, Sheen did not remain in the ivory tower of academia. Known for his skills as an orator, Sheen expanded his reach through a weekly radio program, The Catholic Hour, starting in 1930 and lasting for about twenty-two years with an estimated audience of four million listeners.

In 1951, Fulton Sheen was consecrated as an Auxiliary Bishop of the Archdiocese of New York. That same year, he started his weekly television program, Life is Worth Living, which is probably what he is most known for today. Within a couple of months, the number of stations carrying his program jumped from three to fifteen. “Over the course of the show, Sheen’s Life is Worth Living competed for airtime with popular television stars such as Frank Sinatra and Milton Berle. . . . and in 1953, just two years after its debut, he won an Emmy Award for ‘Most Outstanding Television Personality.’” Apparently, his show, which ran until 1957, had a weekly viewership of a staggering 30 million!

On October 21, 1956, Bishop Sheen appeared on a popular game show What’s My Line? as a mystery guest. The purpose was to raise money for 300 leper colonies run by the Society for the Propagation of the Faith, for which Sheen became the director in 1958.

From 1961 to 1969, “he hosted another popular television show, The Bishop Fulton Sheen Show.” In the middle of that time period, he participated in every session of the Second Vatican Council (1962–1965). According to the CUA website, “he worked closely with then Father Joseph Ratzinger, who was a theological expert on the commission for mission.” During Ratzinger’s tenure as pope, he spoke of how “‘Fulton Sheen . . . would fascinate us in the evenings with his talks.’” Benedict XVI declared Fulton Sheen “Venerable” in July 2012. 

Following the council, Sheen was appointed as Bishop of Rochester, NY, in 1966, serving until 1969 when he resigned at the age of seventy-four, a year before the standard retirement age. As Matthew McDonald reports, “Sheen’s three years in Rochester were difficult.” He had tried to donate “a lightly attended inner-city parish church and its land for a federal public housing project for poor people,” but it “drew so much opposition that parishioners threw pebbles at his car when he visited.”
Word on Fire’s Liturgy of the Hours is Here!
Order Your Set Today

A man of principle, he received backlash from the right and the left. On the one hand, Bishop Sheen met with resistance from the local faithful who did not agree with his manner of implementing the reforms of Vatican II. On the other, “he also drew fire when he defended Pope Paul VI’s anti-contraception encyclical Humanae Vitae,” McDonald notes. Additionally, he was against the United States of America’s involvement in the Vietnam War as well as strongly opposed to Communism.

After his resignation from Rochester, he was named titular Archbishop of Newport, Wales. “From 1976 until his death three years later,” according to Encyclopedia Britannica, “Sheen served Pope Paul VI as assistant to the Pontifical Throne. . . . he died shortly after open-heart surgery in 1979 at the age of 84.”

Fulton J. Sheen’s work and legacy extend far beyond his mass media presence. As CUA records: “He published 34 books during his 23-year teaching career . . . and another 32 after he left the University.” A list of these books, in chronological order of publication, can be found here. Furthermore, “he also was a syndicated columnist in the secular press.”

Sheen’s public notoriety, however, is not even the most admirable aspect of his sanctity. “Admirers of Sheen see markers of holiness throughout his life, including his charity (he gave away millions in royalties, salary and gifts); his concern for troubled souls (he would drop everything to help a single person in need); and his Holy Hour, a 60-minute time in prayer before the Blessed Sacrament that he performed every day,” writes McDonald.

Ven. Fulton J. Sheen’s charity and good work did not end with his death. As a standard requirement for beatification, a miraculous healing has been attributed to his intercession. As reported by Joseph Pronechen, the miracle occurred on September 16, 2010. A baby boy had been stillborn to parents Travis and Bonnie Engstrom from Peoria, IL. The family and friends of the baby’s parents had been imploring Archbishop Fulton Sheen’s intercession since the birth began. Two medical professionals present at the home-birth tried to provide emergency help, but nothing was working. The boy’s father conducted an emergency baptism, naming him James Fulton, after the late bishop. The infant was rushed to the hospital, “where medical professionals tried every possibility to revive and save him. But with no pulse or sign of life after 61 minutes, and doctors about to record his time of death, James [Fulton] came to life.”

While the doctors were obviously astounded at this miraculous return to life, they still gave a poor prognosis. They said that, because he must have suffered “massive organ damage . . . [he] would soon die,” writes Pronechon. When that did not happen either, they were certain he would at least be “severely handicapped.” Afterall, an MRI showed brain damage from the lack of oxygen. Yet, three months later, at a follow-up examination, his brain scans were normal. Now, eight days after his sixteenth birthday, James Fulton Engstrom and his parents will attend the beatification of the holy archbishop, whose own life has inspired multiple generations of Catholic faithful.

items.title: Tuesday, September 1, 2026
items.author: Bishop Robert Barron
items.summary:
Bishop Robert Barron

Friends, today’s Gospel reports that Jesus came to Capernaum, entered the synagogue on a sabbath, and began to teach.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Bishop Robert Barron

Daily Reading


First Reading
1 Corinthians 2:10b-16

These things God has revealed to us through the Spirit; for the Spirit searches everything, even the depths of God. For what human being knows what is truly human except the human spirit that is within? So also no one comprehends what is truly God’s except the Spirit of God. Now we have received not the spirit of the world, but the Spirit that is from God, so that we may understand the gifts bestowed on us by God. And we speak of these things in words not taught by human wisdom but taught by the Spirit, interpreting spiritual things to those who are spiritual.

Those who are unspiritual do not receive the gifts of God’s Spirit, for they are foolishness to them, and they are unable to understand them because they are spiritually discerned. Those who are spiritual discern all things, and they are themselves subject to no one else’s scrutiny.

“For who has known the mind of the Lord
    so as to instruct him?”

But we have the mind of Christ.

Psalm
Psalm 145:8-14

The Lord is gracious and merciful,
    slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love.
The Lord is good to all,
    and his compassion is over all that he has made.
All your works shall give thanks to you, O Lord,
    and all your faithful shall bless you.
They shall speak of the glory of your kingdom,
    and tell of your power,
to make known to all people your mighty deeds,
    and the glorious splendor of your kingdom.
Your kingdom is an everlasting kingdom,
    and your dominion endures throughout all generations.
The Lord is faithful in all his words,
    and gracious in all his deeds.
The Lord upholds all who are falling,
    and raises up all who are bowed down.

Gospel Reading
Luke 4:31-37

He went down to Capernaum, a city in Galilee, and was teaching them on the sabbath. They were astounded at his teaching, because he spoke with authority. In the synagogue there was a man who had the spirit of an unclean demon, and he cried out with a loud voice, “Let us alone! What have you to do with us, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are, the Holy One of God.” But Jesus rebuked him, saying, “Be silent, and come out of him!” When the demon had thrown him down before them, he came out of him without having done him any harm. They were all amazed and kept saying to one another, “What kind of utterance is this? For with authority and power he commands the unclean spirits, and out they come!” And a report about him began to reach every place in the region.

Reflection

Friends, today’s Gospel reports that Jesus came to Capernaum, entered the synagogue on a sabbath, and began to teach. So far, so ordinary. Any bar-mitzvahed adult had the privilege of speaking in synagogue and commenting on the Scripture.

But then it says that the people “were astonished at his teaching because he spoke with authority.” Once again, we’d probably pass over this rather quickly, but it meant the world to a first-century Jew. The ordinary teachers would have appealed to their own teachers and authorities, and finally to Moses and the Torah, which were unassailable.

The Sermon on the Mount gives a wonderful example of Jesus’s authoritative teaching. He appears as the new Moses. Like Moses, he goes up on a mountain, and like Moses, he brings down a kind of new law. But here the comparisons get strained, for Jesus does something that even Moses could never do: He claims authority over the Torah itself. “You have heard it said . . . but I say.” 

What he means is that they have heard it said in the Torah! And this was the authority beyond which there was no appeal. That’s why the people “were astonished at his teaching.”
